doc.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997

title: Honorary recognition from Fredonia and love of classical music
summary: The alumni commendation, his clinic work, and his wish to sing opera; Noto's wife now plays Pavarotti.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Being honored: NEA Jazz Masters and other awards

blocks.x: “You wouldn’t even let me back in and now—”

And here comes, and when they called, I said, “Who is this?” And I thought it was some sort of a put on. But I went there and I very graciously received it, with a great deal of thanks, and everybody went up and gave ten, fifteen minute speeches, and I got up in front of them and I had a drink of water and I looked at them and I held it up and I said, “I just want you to know how thrilled I am about this, and it’s not for what I’ve already done. I promise you it’s going to be for what I’m going to do.”
I think you’re making good on that. Applause please.

And I do. I get out there and I’m very energetic and I give a thousand and one percent to clinics and symposiums and master classes that I give. I mean there’s not anything that I can’t help them with. And so be it. And if I can help spread not just jazz music but music in general — I’m a classical music fanatic — I would give up every note I’ve ever played © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
or written, if I could just once sing the first act of La Boehme in the style of Jussi Bjorling or Pavarotti.
Well you can’t. I’m afraid you have too many good things on record. You can’t give them up.

I would. I’d give it all up if God came down right now and touched me on the shoulder and put that tenor voice up here where it belongs you know, in that nasal passage, in a minute it would be over. No question.

He has influenced my wife because my wife used to listen to jazz records. Now I walk in the house and there’s like Luciano Pavarotti on. He gave her the records. It’s constant. I mean I love it you know, but it’s constant and she used to be a jazz freak, you know, loved jazz.
Well I guess, as Ellington said, “There’s good music and bad music.” Did he say that? He said a lot of things. It sounds like something he might have said.
Yeah, I think he did say it, yeah.
